utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-54-T, the Prosecutor versus Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nice, you're for the OTP, and who is with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Today I am assisted by Ms. Dicklich as ever, Mr. Coo, Ms. Kotseva, Ms. Dragulev, Ms. Rebecca Graham and Mr. Randall, all of whom have been involved at various times in various ways in the exercise of trying to obtain documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And for Serbia and Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: MR. OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on behalf of the government of Serbia and Montenegro, today we have the honour of appearing before you, and we are Mr. Svetislav Rabrenovic, secretary in the office of National Council for Cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal; then we have Mr. Vladimir Cvetkovic, as of recently a colleague of mine in the embassy of Serbia and Montenegro in The Hague and who personally acted upon a request from the Prosecution in a matter we'll be discussing today and he will be able to tell you more about it and expound our positions. My name is Sasa Obradovic. I'm the first secretary of the embassy of Serbia and Montenegro in The Hague. Your Honour, I should like to take advantage of this opportunity right at the outset of this morning's session to request that the discussion about the documents be conducted in closed session, or private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have motions filed by the Prosecution for relief under Rule 54 bis, and we also have a motion for protective measures filed by the government of Serbia and Montenegro. Today's hearing will last approximately an hour. Each side will have 20 minutes to present its arguments, and we'll also set aside time for a reply and for any other ancillary matters. The Chamber had directed the parties to focus their attention on certain issues which we identified, and I expect the submissions to be so focused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, may I just seek a clarification from you. Are you asking that the entire hearing be in private session or just those portions of it in which reference may be made or will be made to the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for asking the question. It's a technical one. At this point in time, bearing in mind the confidentiality of these proceedings and the confidential information that both sides have presented in their written submissions, we are not in a position in advance to foresee when and how long we're going to need to go into private session. That is why we should like to request that the entire session this morning be held in private session, closed to the public, so that we can freely present our views and positions, which don't only have to do with confidential documents which the Prosecution is seeking from us but relate to the confidentiality of the proceedings and relationship and cooperation between the organs of Serbia and Montenegro in these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OBRADOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I had intended to start in open session, if there was no objection, but I can recognise that it may be quite difficult to partition the hearing out between those parts that need protection and those that don't, because many of the filings that would be referred to or may be referred to are of themselves confidential, as is the underlying material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have the hearing in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Kostic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, where we left off, you said that this session of Slovenia entailed fewer problems because there were no inter-ethnic conflicts in Slovenia. I wanted us to look at the comments on that topic by Borisav Jovic in this film, and I asked for that short clip to be played. Can it be done now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is a problem with the sound.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There should be sound. This is something different, nothing to do with my clip. I would like them to play Jovic with sound.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] At the same time it means a lot of destruction and a lot of victims. "[Previous translation continues] ... the attack. All they needed was the nod from the most powerful republic, Serbia, but they were in for a surprise. "I said very clearly then that it's pointless to discuss and disagree with Slovenes and to wage war with them because the Slovene situation is clear. They have an ethnically pure republic, no territorial disputes. "It doesn't bother us at all if they leave Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The rest does not bear on the topic. So, Jovic said the same as you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Jovic also said that there were no inter-ethnic or civil disputes in Slovenia. The problem of war did not arise, and the problem was much simpler, generally speaking, because the population was homogenous. I believe over 95 per cent of Slovenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is clear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I want to point out to you, Mr. Robinson, this translation is completely wrong, because Jovic does not say at any point that Serbia had no interest in it. That is again a forgery. We were not able to hear it. If you really want to hear what was said, let the interpreters interpret what he said in the Serbian language, and what was written in the subtitles is absolutely not correct. This is not the first example of this. It just goes to show that this entire series is completely falsified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All we have, though, is the translation by the interpreter, which is accurate, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not listen to the interpretation. I listened to what Jovic said in Serbian, but I looked at the subtitles in English, and it's completely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the interpretation into English in the transcript does not make any reference to Serbia. So you shouldn't be concerned about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm concerned about the fact that this was exhibited, whereas the translation in subtitles is completely wrong. You could see that back when Mr. Nice played a film in which you can see what I was saying about Kosovo Polje and the translation was completely incorrect. Mr. Robinson made interpreters do it and redo it twice in order to show that the subtitles were completely wrong. But let us move on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please, Professor Kostic, tell us very briefly what happened at the Ohrid meeting and what was written in the Ohrid peace declaration of the 22nd of July, 1992 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ohrid meeting was attended by the full Presidency of the SFRY and all presidents of republics or, alternatively, presidents of Presidencies of republics of the former Yugoslavia. The Ohrid declaration that was adopted at that time, true in the absence of Mr. Tudjman who walked out on that session, appealed to the same principles that the European Community upheld at the time and that we in the Presidency had agreed and harmonised several times, the same principles that we at the session of the Presidency of the 5th of September agreed unanimously and which Mr. Mesic presented at the inaugural conference of The Hague peace conference on the 7th September in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 20 --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour. There is a mistake in the transcript. We are talking about the Ohrid declaration and it's 1991, but in the transcript it says 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. That's noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in tab 20, you have this Ohrid declaration. We are not going through the entire text. It says: "We have to put a stop to the use of force which has taken human lives and continues to do so and moves us ever further from our vital interests. These interests are democratic development, respect for individual and collective rights and civil liberties. All this can be achieved only in peace. We, the participants in this meeting between war and peace, declare that we are unanimously and categorically in favour of peace." This is basically the spirit of the Ohrid meeting and declaration. Is that expressed here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then in the penultimate paragraph, it says: "The president of the SFRY Presidency, Stjepan Mesic, and the president of the Republic of Croatia, Dr. Franjo Tudjman, demanded the unconditional withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army to garrisons, which was not accepted by the majority of participants in this meeting and hence they have not assented to including this in the text of the statement." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Mesic both continued insisting that the Yugoslav People's Army should withdraw into its barracks, and at the same time they obstructed the decisions and conclusions adopted several times by the SFRY Presidency to first disarm all the paramilitary units whose number already exceeded the total number of JNA personnel in the whole territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What paramilitary units are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the police force in Croatia over two months increased from 17.000 to 19.000. In addition to that, the Home Guards Corps was set up. We're still talking about the time when Yugoslavia was one country, all the system was functioning, all the institutions. The JNA and the Territorial Defence were the only legal armed forces. At that time, Croatia set up the Home Guards Corps, the ZNG, and then they massively armed them and their citizens with illegally smuggled arms. They armed members of the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union, on the basis of their political affiliation. And of course, withdrawing the JNA into barracks at the time when there was serious tensions and inter-ethnic conflicts in certain areas of Croatia, especially those areas with majority Serb population, withdraw of the JNA into barracks would have certainly met physical destruction of the Serb people in those territories and complete ethnic cleansing. Let me point out this: Because of the refusal of Croatia and Slovenia, and later some other republics, to send their recruits to the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army was decimated practically, in terms of personnel. And with the available personnel, we were unable to protect the population in Western Slavonia using the army. What happened to that population? Since we were unable, we did not have the capacity to put the army there to act as a buffer, Croatian units ethnically cleansed those areas, first 28 villages and then the rest. They torched all their houses, destroyed all their property, and created a situation which made it impossible for anyone to return. That was still 1991 when Croatia -- when Croatia was still acting as it acted within Yugoslavia as a single state, and it lasted until the 27th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did the Presidency do to stop the conflicts in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did a lot. We adopted a lot of conclusions, but few were implemented. We came out with many communiques, adopted a lot of conclusions, made appeals and noted frequently that the leadership of Croatia and Croatian paramilitary units do not abide by a single cease-fire agreement. They were blocking the barracks of the JNA which were stationed there according to peacetime establishment. Barracks were under blockade. Power could not be supplied, food, and other necessities. Parents gathered around the barracks. Parents of the officers of the Yugoslav People's Army gathered outside the barracks to appeal to their children to surrender. Such an inappropriate attitude to the JNA as the legitimate armed force of the SFRY would not have been suffered by any other army or any other military leadership the way it was suffered by the military leadership of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did there ever come a proposal about the future of Yugoslavia prepared by the Presidency commission? I believe it was on the 5th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have already mentioned that agreement. Later, it grew into a harmonised proposal by the entire SFRY Presidency, and we in the Presidency, chaired by Mr. Stjepan Mesic, had agreed to present that agreement through Mr. Stjepan Mesic at the inaugural meeting in The Hague of the peace conference on 7th September, 1991. There were four basic principles that were agreed and harmonised, and Mr. Stjepan Mesic presented them at that conference. The first, respect of every nation's right to self-determination, including the right to secession and forming unions. Two, democratic expression of the will of every nation and republic to exercise their status in keeping with their real interests. Third, the principle of equality that constitutes equality of all options. No imposition of anyone's will and no use of force. Four, the principle of legality, which is -- which presupposes that political agreement should be legalised and a procedure instituted for its implementation. Every solution should be equal and reasonable, acceptable to all, and it should be implemented with mutual agreement and democratically. Mr. Mesic writes about these principles on page 226 of his book. In order not to take too much of your time, if you look at these principles carefully, these four principles were all seriously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The basic question I asked you was what did the SFRY Presidency do to stop the war in Croatia? I'll make it more specific. How many decisions on cease-fire were adopted by the SFRY Presidency? How many agreements on cease-fire involved the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over about eight months the Presidency adopted 14 cease-fire agreements. Each of them, even when they did not directly involve the Presidency, included Mr. Veljko Kadijevic, federal secretary for national defence. And every time before a cease-fire agreement was concluded, Mr. Kadijevic was authorised by the Presidency to take part in this work and to conclude a cease-fire agreement. Regrettably, although each of these agreements required two pre-conditions; immediate cease-fire, and as a second point the obligation of Croatia to lift the blockade of JNA barracks, and I said earlier that over 1.000 army personnel was blocked in those barracks, the Croatian authorities never complied. A very specific conclusion of this kind was also adopted by The Hague Conference on the 18th of October, attended by all eight members of the Presidency. It was also attended by Mr. Tudjman and by you, Mr. Milosevic, by Mr. Cyrus Vance, Lord Carrington, Mr. Hans van den Broek. It was also unanimously adopted by the SFRY Presidency to have a cease-fire, but then already on the 5th of November, 1991, at the next Hague Conference, Lord Carrington began the session by saying that the conclusions of the 18th of September were not observed and the -- Croatia did not abide by the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there some -- was there some pattern into it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pattern was that the Croatian authorities unlawfully became renegades from the Yugoslav constitution. They threw out the Serb people from their own constitution, whereas the Serb population of Croatia expressed their desire to observe, to abide by the Yugoslav constitution and to remain within Yugoslavia. In this conflict, the Croatian authorities tried to impose their will on the Serbs in Croatia by use of force. I don't have to invent any of this. Mr. Mesic himself says in his book that every time Croatia launched an initiative or an action, a reaction followed by the other side. The indictment refers to it as the Serbian Bloc, where I say that it cannot be called a Serbian Bloc. It can only be called supporters of the Yugoslav option. So every action of Serbs in Croatia was provoked by prior action of the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you said about the Serb bloc, that it's a misnomer, it should be called supporters of the Yugoslav option, was that something you were advocating or was it the valid constitutional arrangement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the valid constitutional arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it your constitutional obligation to protect it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was our constitutional obligation. Not only of us who were in favour of preserving Yugoslavia, but those who opted for secession as well. I told Mr. Drnovsek and Mr. Mesic at the time that their behaviour and their engagement and their work in those days, despite the fact that they signed and gave the same oath at the federal parliament as I did, their behaviour cannot be qualified otherwise but treason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout this time -- you were at the head of the Presidency until mid-1992, for quite a long time after the peacekeeping forces arrived and all conflicts were halted. Throughout this time, did a situation arise in which the JNA carried out an action, first initiated an action, or did it only respond to what the Croatian forces were doing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA took no offensive action at that time. I was one of those who very often spoke out in public to say that if the Croatian armed formations and the Croatian authorities, even after so many cease-fires and even after having undertaken so many times to lift the blockade of the JNA barracks, failed to carry out this obligation, I will advocate that the JNA finally take offensive action and lift the blockade on the JNA barracks by force. Not to take over territory or to take over Croatian towns, but simply to use force to enable our soldiers to be taken out of those blocked barracks. Only in the area of Karlovac did the JNA move forward, did it advance, but it only reached the outskirts of the town. And I think that that barracks was liberated through fighting. What was happening in the areas of Dubrovnik and Vukovar in my deep conviction was a very firm commitment by the Croatian leadership to spread the flames of war to other territories in Yugoslavia. Dubrovnik borders with Montenegro, and Vukovar is on the border with Serbia. We had military barracks in both areas. The effort of the Croatian leadership was aimed at spreading the flames of war to Montenegro, Serbia, and Bosnia. I think that through its decisive action, both on the territory of Dubrovnik and the territory of Vukovar, the JNA prevented Tudjman from carrying out this intention. Unfortunately, however, we did not manage to stop the spreading of the flames of war to Bosnia-Herzegovina, primarily because of areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina, mainly in Western Herzegovina, but also in Posavina, bordering with Croatia, were inhabited primarily by Croats, so that the paramilitary formations from Croatia could infiltrate the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina through these Croat inhabited areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, what you have just explained now, was this the main characteristic of the engagement of the JNA on Croatian territory while you, as part of the Presidency, were part of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was what the JNA engagement was all about. What it says in this indictment is all topsy-turvy. Had we had a plan to create a Greater Serbia, had there been some kind of secret joint criminal enterprise, the Rump Presidency, as they called it, would not have called on the United Nations to send its peacekeeping forces on that territory in order to withdraw the JNA from those areas and avoid further conflict. The main purpose of calling on the peacekeeping forces was for them to protect the Serb population which had, up 'til that time, been protected by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, what was the longest period that any of the contingents of the JNA were blockaded in barracks? Can you give me an example of one that was blockaded for a lengthy period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To tell you the truth, I couldn't give you any precise information right now, but I think that the barracks in Sisak, Karlovac, Jastrebarsko near Zagreb, and some other peacetime locations remained under blockade for quite a long time, as did the barracks in the Vukovar, until a really serious conflict broke out there between the JNA and the Croatian paramilitary formations. I think, if I'm correct, it lasted three or four months if not five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So several months, you say.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that some barracks were blocked for as long as seven months, because the final lifting of the blockade and the withdrawal from the barracks on the territory of Croatia took place only after the last cease-fire was signed in which Mr. Cyrus Vance participated. This was one of the pre-conditions for the peacekeeping forces to be deployed in Croatia, and that was already in January or February 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell me, then, what was your principal motivation as a member of the Presidency in not directing the army to take action to remove these blockades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you that. We were aware that issuing such an order to the JNA, which had artillery, projectiles, an air force, and so on and so forth, but the Croatian side had more armed men. The JNA, however, was far superior in technology and weaponry. Therefore, had the JNA initiated offensive action in order to reach all those towns and lift the blockade of the barracks through fighting, this would have involved large-scale destruction, possible large-scale civilian casualties among the population, and possibly casualties among our own soldiers. The only reason that prevented us from issuing such an order was the desire to achieve this aim through peaceful means and save people's lives. There was 14 cease-fires. After each one, we expected the Croatian leadership and armed formations to finally agree to lift the blockade on the barracks without fighting. Mr. Bonomy, I have to tell you that we were under intense moral pressure. I myself was under intense moral pressure as a member of the Supreme Command. There was pressure from the mothers and parents not to mobilise new conscripts, but we also had to bear in mind the fate of the conscripts who were living in those barracks in conditions worse than those in concentration camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Who broke the cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, we were all in the Presidency. It was the Presidency of the SFRY that negotiated the cease-fires. We were the civilian Supreme Command. When an imminent threat of war was declared on the 1st of October -- may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Just tell me briefly, can you, how were the cease-fires broken and who broke them? Or is it brokered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every time --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, there's been a misunderstanding. Your question was who broke the cease-fire. However, the interpretation that the witness heard was who agreed the cease-fires.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that while the Presidency was working in its full composition it issued decisions on the cease-fires and agreed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What I'm interested in finding out is not who made the cease-fires, how they came about, but how they came to an end. Who broke or breached the cease-fires?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every time, they were broken by the paramilitary formations of Croatia, as I said yesterday, with abundant assistance from outside. Everything was done to continue the war clashes, because this was the only way that Croatian territory could be freed of the Serbian population living there. I can show you several statements issued by the staff of the Supreme Command stating who had broken the cease-fire and how. If we have time, we can look at a tab containing statements after the 18th of October, after the joint session at The Hague Conference, which was attended by all the members of the Presidency and the decision on a cease-fire was issued. After this, we have statements by the Supreme Command and the Presidency of the SFRY that only 24 or 36 hours later Croatian paramilitary formations breached the cease-fire 124 times. There were 124 violations which large numbers of soldiers killed on the JNA side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the session of the SFRY Presidency of the 1st of October, 1992 [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who participated in that session?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six members of the Presidency. Only Mr. Drnovsek and Mr. Mesic were missing. The representatives of Croatia of Slovenia, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that session attended by six members of the Presidency and held on the 1st of October, was any evaluation made of the situation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried more than once to convene a session of the Presidency before the 1st of September [as interpreted], but we could not do so because Mr. Mesic kept obstructing, failing to turn up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the transcript's becoming a bit of a mix-up, I think. This is October of 1991, I think, not 1992, and we started off talking about a meeting on the 1st of October and now the transcript is talking about the 1st of September. So ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, we are talking about the meeting of the Presidency of the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1991. I only wanted to say that previously there had been several unsuccessful attempts to hold a meeting of the Presidency, because the leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina insisted that the Presidency meet as soon as possible due to the highly dangerous situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We were unable to gather all the members of the Presidency, and we finally met on the 1st of October, 1991, in the composition I have just described. Six members were present, and only Mr. Drnovsek of Slovenia and Mr. Mesic of Croatia were absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what conclusions did you arrive at on the 1st of October?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we had several times previously, we again concluded that the security situation was extremely difficult, that there was an imminent threat of war and civil war, but for the first time we concluded that the country was actually in an imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this was the session where the Presidency for the first time concluded that there was an imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a unanimous decision of all six members of the Presidency, which constituted the two-thirds majority required by the rules of procedure of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, was there actually an imminent threat of war in the state?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only was there an imminent threat of war, there was already a war going on with the paramilitary formations of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have just explained this. On the 1st of October, six members of the Presidency, with a two-thirds majority, issued a conclusion that the country was facing an imminent threat of war, and you say, and this is not in dispute, that there actually was a war already going on. In these indictments, and also we have heard from some witnesses about the Rump Presidency. Have you heard this expression?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what some media called it.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only the media but also the leadership of the secessionist republics. They kept using this term. Not only that, but they openly stated that we had in this way perpetrated a military coup; a coup d'etat, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the legal basis after the Presidency, with a two-thirds majority, concluded that the country was facing an imminent threat of war? What was the legal basis for the continuation of the work of the Presidency in this composition?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Tito died in 1980, this problem arose. The problem of extreme nationalism and inter-ethnic conflict existed before. They did not arise only in the 1990s. So that in 1984, the Presidency of the SFRY issued a special decision amending the rules on the work of -- on the procedure of the Presidency. And according to this decision, if there was an imminent threat of war, the Presidency could meet regardless of whether it had the necessary majority to issue decisions. Two, three, or four members of the Presidency could hold a session if the others were unable to attend or were absent, and they could issue valid decisions, qualified legal decisions. So that constitutionally, the Presidency was authorised to issue decree laws if the parliament was unable to meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's find the link in that chain now and see whether it follows a logical evolution of events. On the 1st of October, you, within a two-thirds majority, assessed that the country was in a state of imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After 1984, you have a rules of procedure for the Presidency where it says that when there is imminent threat of war, the Presidency works with as many members as it has. So those are two points.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that the legal grounds for continuing the work of the Presidency in any composition?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 63 of the Bosnian indictment, it says that: "On the 3rd of October of 1991, four members of the Presidency of the SFRY from Serbia Montenegro -" it says Borisav Jovic, Jugoslav Kostic, doesn't mention Kosovo and Vojvodina here, Sejdo Bajramovic, Ibrahim Kostic, the three of them, therefore, and you yourself - "assumed the function of the SFRY Presidency circumventing the roles and responsibilities of the Presidency members from Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Macedonia." Now, please, explain this to us. Since this is what it says there, I've read it out to you, it's paragraph 63 of the BH indictment, does this mean taking over the function of the SFRY Presidency, or was it a case of the legal performing of that function by its legally elected members?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the observation made and the formulation as it stands in the indictment is completely incorrect and wrong. It was not a matter of assuming the function of the SFRY Presidency, taking over its function, but it was continuing the work of the Presidency in its functioning in a legal, constitutional manner on the basis of assessments made that a state of imminent war existed, which the Presidency made according to its rules of procedure at a previous meeting on the 1st of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean the 1st of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, what happened? Because it says on the 3rd of October 1991 the four members of the SFRY Presidency, et cetera, assumed the function. What happened on at that day the 3rd of October, the date quoted in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, immediately after the 1st of October, we had intended to hold a new meeting of the Presidency on the 2nd of October, and I was personally called up by Mr. Bogic Bogicevic and Mr. Vasil Tupurkovski, and they asked me defer the meeting to the 3rd of October, to postpone it. And I consulted the other members of the Presidency and accepted their proposal. So we convened that meeting for the 3rd of October, we scheduled it for the 3rd of October. However, neither Mr. Tupurkovski nor Mr. Bogicevic turned up on the 3rd of October, and of course faced with a situation of that kind we had -- could do nothing else but, on the basis of what we had already established and assessed on the 1st of October, that we go on with a normal session on the 3rd of October. Now, Their Honours, the Judges, don't have enough patience ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is on the transcript there? Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness interrupted when he saw you conferring, so he thought it best to stop what he was saying, to have you hold your consultations after which he could resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness, you were interrupted in giving your explanation.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I thought it was very important for the Judges to hear this detail that I'm going to present regardless of the fact that they don't have all the patience to hear all the details which convincingly speak of the fact that there was no plan for a Greater Serbia nor was there any joint enterprise afoot but what was afoot was the existence of a plan on the violent secession by the protagonists of that secession against the constitution. And this is one of the details which I think is very important for you to hear and which will show how much even the most obvious matters are being distorted and shown to be in an untruthful matter. And here it is: Mr. Mesic, speaking about the 1st of October and speaking about the 3rd of October, said that we had conducted a military putsch. Mr. Mesic says quite literally, and I'm quoting him here, the following. We can find that in page 269 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's tab 73.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, tab 73, but it's easier for me to follow it in my book. This is what Mr. Mesic says: "However, on the 1st of October the situation of an imminent threat of war was not mentioned but what is stated in the statement as well, the Presidency of the SFRY of the competent federal organs was informed that the political security and safety situation in the country was highly serious and dramatic, and that there was the threat of an all-out civil war from breaking out." And Mr. Mesic goes on to say: "In the statement, there is no mention of an imminent threat of war and on the basis of that we can see that invitation to a previous session was forgery, was false, but this cabinet went on with the decision that their function and action was not falsely presented." And he's referring to us who supported the Yugoslav option. Now, in that same statement that was published by Tanjug on the 1st of October, both for the international public and for the domestic public, which is quoted by Mr. Mesic himself only eight lines below what he's just quoted, it says the following, quite literally: "It was assessed that there was obvious -- that there was the obvious danger of armed conflicts expanding to Bosnia-Herzegovina and engulfing Montenegro as well whereby new areas of conflict would be opened in the country." And then, from the statement published in Tanjug on the 1st of October, it says: "It was assessed that this was a serious threat and would create even more serious inter -- inter-ethnic conflicts and that Yugoslavia was facing a war -- the danger of a war." Now, Your Honours, Judges, if we have such obvious matters on such important matters such as the 1st of October Presidency decision which Mr. Mesic and this indictment attempts to portray as being a putsch, and if such untruths and obvious falsities are presented, then you can only assume how many -- how much falsehood there is and untruths there are in Mr. Mesic's books and in his statements and in the indictment itself, because the authors of the indictment quite obviously did not take the trouble to compile the indictment both in Belgrade and Sarajevo and Podgorica and Ljubljana and Skopje but they compiled and drafted it in Zagreb and they made a plagiarism of Mesic's book but Mesic calls us, those of us who were in favour of the Yugoslav option, he calls us the four-member band or group -- gang of four, and the gentleman compiling the indictment referred to us as the undertakers of a joint criminal enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question to which that interminable answer related was what happened on the 3rd of October. Can I take you back just slightly on that to the 1st of October. Is there a tab here in which we see recorded the decision of the 1st of October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there is. In my book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. A formal document. Is there a decision of the Presidency, properly recorded, minuted decision about the imminent state of war and, therefore, a determination that it was appropriate for a meeting to take place and decisions to be made by smaller numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, Mr. Kostic quoted the decision in very precise terms in his book. I don't have the original document here, just as I don't have many other original documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But Mr. Mesic's complaint seems to be that the decision wasn't properly recorded, and what I'd like to see is the record. Now, it seems such a major, important decision that one might expect it to be available to the Tribunal in its proper formal form. Now, are you telling me you don't have it, and we've just to look at books written by people for the material?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, a decision is one thing, a decision by which the Yugoslav state Presidency in 1984 regulated the question of how and in what way the Presidency should function under conditions of an imminent threat of war, and in that sense I mentioned that decision as the grounds, the legal grounds and framework for the continuance of the work of the Yugoslav state Presidency. However, in that decision no mention is made of any separate decisions nor is there the obligation of bringing in separate decisions, but at the time when the Presidency assesses, evaluates, therefore, that the country is indeed facing imminent war, then at that point in time the Presidency starts functioning under such conditions. Now, you're asking of me -- or, rather, to do that whereas the OTP can come by those documents more easily than I can. But it's not a question of somebody writing that down in a book. It is an official statement which was published by Tanjug, the Yugoslav news agency, on the 1st of October 1991 for the domestic public and the international public. And in my book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in my book you have literally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I follow that. But, Mr. Kostic, we are bombarded in this Trial Chamber by official documents of various state organs of various parts of the former Yugoslavia, and it seems to be a trait that the most minute decisions are recorded in some formal document, and here we have a massive decision that there is an imminent threat of war and a much reduced composition of the Presidency can act in that situation. Are you telling me that you don't in that situation make a formal record for the federal record purposes of the assessment that that was the situation and that therefore a smaller number of the Presidency could act?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, we are discussing two matters here. Quite obviously, I'm not a lawyer myself and I can't discuss it on a par with you in the legal sense when it comes to this matter, but a moment ago you said yourself that Mr. Mesic was objecting and saying that a decision had not been taken. I think that's what you said a moment ago, words to that effect, whereas I didn't address those complaints and objections by Mr. Mesic. All I was saying is that Mr. Mesic was claiming that in the statement that I quoted, there was no mention of an imminent threat of war being in existence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and he's quoting that passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But could you answer my question: Is there no formal decision written down and kept in the archives, federal archives at that time, by the Presidency - at least the numbers that were able to assemble - that there was an imminent threat of war and that therefore future decisions could be made by a smaller number? Is there no formal record kept of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said a moment ago that there is the decision about how the Presidency functions and makes decisions in circumstances of that kind. But in that 1984 decision, it was just an assessment of there being an imminent threat of war situation. I don't think there's a separate decision because there was no need for a separate decision to exist because the situation -- an assessment of the situation was brought in in the presence of six Presidency members on the 1st of October. It was these people who assessed that situation as being such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand -- I understand all of that, and I understand that we can all -- the people who were there can all write books about it, give their versions, but it would be nice to have the formal record just to confirm it. Anyway, it doesn't look as though it exists from your answer, so let's move to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will take the first break at 11.00 for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] L.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, is this assessment, this appraisal of the existence of a situation of the imminent threat of war, was that established on the 1st of October, and was it published in an official communique or official statement issued by the Presidency after having held that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you quoted, is that the official statement, the official communique of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the official communique broadcast by Tanjug. In 1992 I had already withdrew from political life -- withdrawn from political life. I wasn't in a position to be able to come by such documentation, but this is the original text quoted by me and published and broadcast by Tanjug on the basis of an official Presidency communique.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is that the official Presidency communique statement where it states what you said, that the country was faced with imminent threat of war, was it published and printed, not just an agency piece of news, a news item by Tanjug?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, it was officially published.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the printed media, the electronic media, and that same communique and statement as quoted by Mr. Kostic can be found in the newspapers of the 2nd of October, and that, too, is a public document because the Presidency thereby informed the public about the position it had taken.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a recording of the entire press conference held at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course you do. But the essential point is, is that how it was made public from the Presidency meeting? Was that an official Presidency communique that you gave?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall do my best to get hold of a copy of the newspapers and to attach that as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now with respect to the quotation from paragraph 63 that I read out, and I don't wish to read it out again, the four of you, did you go beyond the duties of -- and go beyond what the members of Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Macedonia do? Did you circumvent the roles and responsibilities of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All the meetings, including the 3rd of October session and all the following Presidency sessions, not only Mr. Mesic as president but all the members of the Presidency received invitations to attend. They received all the accompanying documents. They were regularly informed, and even if Mr. President does claim that it was a putsch, that -- whereby we excommunicated the other Presidency members, I should just like to remind you of the fact that 15 days after that, in The Hague, a meeting of the Presidency of the FRY was held before The Hague Conference and at that Presidency meeting it was Mr. Mesic that presided over the meeting as president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So two weeks after that 3rd of October date, when you allegedly went ahead and went -- and conducted a putsch, he chaired a Presidency meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And not only that, but asked by journalists whether he was the new -- whether I was the new Presidency president, I said no. I said if Mr. Mesic were to appear tomorrow, he would preside over the Presidency meetings as president, but if he was not present, then in his absence it would be the vice-president who chaired the Presidency meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How about the Presidency members who continued to work; you, Jovic, Bajramovic and Kostic? Did you agree on all issues or was there any disagreement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Far from it. We had differences on many issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But what was the key joint position of those members of the Presidency who continued to work?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our key joint commitment was to preserve Yugoslavia and to work for it, and failing that, to preserve life in a joint state to the extent possible. Second, to find a peaceful solution to the Yugoslav crisis and not to dispute any nation's and any republic's right to self-determination and secession provided it is done in a constitutional and peaceful way. The third issue on which we all found ourselves on the same wavelength was that the Yugoslav People's Army should not be used as a force to topple any government in any republic that was elected at multi- party elections but to use instead the Yugoslav People's Army either as a buffer or as a protector of any nation or part of a nation that finds itself in jeopardy and possibly to lift the blockade of the barracks in Croatia if it is not done otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an example of the differences among the four of you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them were between Mr. Borisav Jovic and me. Of course, not on the four issues on which we all agreed. But otherwise, we had plenty differences. For instance, the election of Mr. Mesic was one thing we didn't agree on. He gave his vote for and I didn't. He had his own convictions and I had to respect them. I think that's only democratic. Also, with regard to the 14 cease-fire agreements, after all of them expired and our soldiers were still blocked, I advocated that the General Staff's proposal to use force to lift the blockade of the barracks should be accepted. Mr. Jovic was against. Also, at the time when we were working in a reduced composition, only the four of us, decisions were made by the Presidency to send into retirement a great number of generals. The first group included 28 generals. The second group was even larger. We did not agree on that. Mr. Jovic calls my engagement in the retirement of these generals insolence. We had other differences as well but they were marginal compared to the important issues on which we did agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, whether you the only member of the Presidency who favoured using force to lift the blockade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to say that Mr. Jugoslav Kostic and Mr. Sejdo Bajramovic, when we discussed this, did not voice their opinions, whereas Mr. Jovic was emphatically against. But again, you see, when we had this disagreement about the retirement of the generals, Mr. Jovic tried everything to bring the issue of the second group of generals back on the agenda, which I categorically refused. The other two members of the Presidency abstained from saying yea or nay, and then I gave my irrevocable resignation to the post of vice-president, telling them I cannot go on working under those conditions, and after that Mr. Jugoslav Kostic and Sejdo Bajramovic both came to see me, confirming that I wasn't doing anything on my own initiative, alone, that they agreed with me. Mr. Jovic was at that time in China. He thought that everything should pass through him, but later he abandoned his demand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Those are examples of your differences. But concerning the main issues, your commitment to preserving Yugoslavia, et cetera, you agreed on that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it also your constitutional obligation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was. Let me also say that concerning the preservation of Yugoslavia, when the first Yugoslavia was established, Serbia and Montenegro were the only recognised states who invested their statehoods into their new -- into that new state. Montenegro had its statehood recognised at the Berlin Congress in 1848, and I fought until the end for preserving that Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will take the break now for 20 minutes. The next break will be at 12.20, or one hour after we -- Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tab 33 is the Presidency statement of 1st of October concerning imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that the one that was said to be 73? The actual statement is 33?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tab 33, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's translated, yes. All right. We'll have a look at it, if necessary, after the resumption. We will break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Professor Kostic, did the Presidency of the SFRY in that composition, after the assessment was made of the imminent threat of war when was Presidency was working in a reduced composition, did it adopt any decisions? Did it adopt a single decision ordering some offensive engagement of the JNA or the armed forces of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that entire period, the Presidency working with four members did not pass a single decision that would order the JNA to take offensive action. Not only that, it did not avail itself of the constitutional possibility to make decrees with the force of law, to abolish political parties, replace leaderships, or to eliminate democratic rights. The Presidency did not adopt a single decision of that kind, although such a constitutional possibility existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the content of the decisions passed by that Presidency? Can we go through them? What are the most important decisions taken by the Presidency in the period we are reviewing, from the 3rd of October onwards?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can go tab by tab, but I could also say simply, very briefly. All the main decisions taken by the Presidency, both in its full composition and its reduced composition, are: The election of Stjepan Mesic as president. The second decision was to dismiss the December class of trained soldiers. The decision on 13 concluded cease-fire agreements and attempts to resolve the Yugoslav crisis by peaceful means. Then the decision to shift to the method of work under conditions of imminent threat of war, which paralysed the highest leadership of the state and the Supreme Command of the JNA, which was the Presidency. The decision to send a request to the Secretary-General of the United Nations and the Security Council to send peace troops, peacekeepers to crisis areas in Croatia to enable the JNA to pull out from those territories. Also, we as the Presidency passed a decision to be the sponsors of the peace conference on Yugoslavia regarding events in Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 3rd of January. Also, the decision on the withdrawal of JNA units and temporary relocation from Slovenia to other areas until a political solution is found. And, of course, our decisions to pull out the Yugoslav People's Army from other territories of the former Yugoslavia at the time when other republics were taking their decisions on independence, such as withdrawal of the JNA from Macedonia, which was carried out without any conflict because there were no Macedonian paramilitaries and no attacks on the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask you, Professor, did the Presidency in its reduced membership have the same powers as the Presidency in its full membership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The Presidency in its full composition had less authority, fewer authorisations than the reduced Presidency. When the Presidency is working under conditions of imminent threat of war, it also assumes in part a legislative role, but we didn't take advantage of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it would have been entitled to order an offensive by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So under circumstances of imminent threat of war, the Presidency can work in its full composition as well, and even as such it has greater authority, greater authorisations. In The Hague, on the 18th of October, the Presidency was in its full composition. It was chaired by Mr. Mesic. But since the conditions were those of imminent threat of war, they had greater authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 65 of the Bosnian indictment, it says: "On the 22nd of October, 1991, or around that date, Slobodan Milosevic, together with other members of the joint criminal enterprise, continued to advocate for a unitary Serb state governed from Belgrade, Serbia. On the same date, the Rump Presidency called for the mobilisation of reservists in Serbia and other regions that want to stay in Yugoslavia." "Other regions" under quotation marks, and the "Rump Presidency" also under quotation marks. Mr. Robinson did not use the term that you heard in the interpretation. He didn't say a "Rump Presidency," he said "reduced."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a better term.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "Reduced" is a correct term, whereas "rump" is derogatory. Tell me, please, can a unitary state in Yugoslavia be the same thing [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear from me or my close associate or any of those people who allegedly were with me in the so-called joint criminal enterprise, did you hear ever from any of us anything about a unitary Serb state?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you comment on this allegation that I, together with other members of that joint criminal enterprise, continued to advocate for a unitary Serb state governed from Belgrade, Serbia? How does it sound to you, that somebody on that day continued something that it seems from other allegations he never stopped doing anyway?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a nonsensical allegation. I can say nothing about it. Maybe the authors of the indictment can better explain what they wanted to say with this. I don't see what you could have continued to do on at that day even if you had been doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For example, during the testimony of academician Kosta Mihailovic, Mr. Nice accused me and the leadership for not accepting the confederate state as proposed by Slovenes and Croats. Similar testimony was given by other witnesses, such as Mesic. What, in your view, was the point of that proposal for confederalisation; and do you believe that this proposal was realistic, acceptable, a serious one?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that even the most prominent protagonists of aggressive secession, the very top echelons of the Slovene and Croatian leadership, have already confirmed in their public statements themselves that the idea of confederalisation was only the first step towards independence and secession from Yugoslavia, the establishment of an independent Croatian state. They persisted on that path. Mr. Tudjman stated publicly that war could have been avoided if they hadn't insisted on an independent Croatia and its secession from Yugoslavia. It would also be good to look at some statements of Mr. Mesic while he was the right hand of Mr. Mesic [as interpreted] in 1992 and 1993 and later president of Croatia, and his very different approach to the issue in 1999 -- sorry, 1990, when he was the leader of the opposition party in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It would be useful to look at that, but before that I want to read to you a brief part of the transcript of Mesic's testimony. Pages 10546 and 10547. "[In English] Slovenia and Croatia, assisted by Bosnia-Herzegovina and Macedonia, we proposed to have a confederal system because the model of a federation as the one that existed could not be sustained. That is what I always emphasise. The three cohesive factors were no longer there. And the only possible thing was a confederacy. However, until the present day, Serbia did not respond to our proposal to opt for a confederal solution, to reach an agreement on this, to come to a consensus and not act through the army and have solutions imposed on us. We could not accept Croatia, Slovenia, and other republics to be treated the way Milosevic treated Vojvodina, Montenegro, and Kosovo. We could not accept that kind of federation, and that is precisely what he wanted, a firm federation. "That is what I wish to say by way of an explanation. What was said was that confederation could not exist. They even said that there was a confederacy in the United States of America. Well, true, but it did not fall apart. But it did function and it -- and there is proof of that." Et cetera. [Interpretation] So he claims in his testimony that he had advocated a confederation, that it was a principled view of theirs, but let us clear up this first. He says that what "he" wanted - he being me - was a firm federation. Did anybody talk about a firm federation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I personally worked for at that time and many times later for a functional federation, not a firm one. For what we have now in Serbia and Montenegro is neither a federation nor a confederation. It is an extremely unfunctional creature. Every union presumes that two entities that are sovereign invest part of that sovereignty into that union and work together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So did I advocate a firm federation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mesic says that their approach was to propose a confederation. Let us look now at his statement given on television regarding the issue. I think it was in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're right, 1999.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in October 1999, on Montenegro TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us play the clip briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The Croatian contribution is this: Croatia had lived for a long time without having a separate state. The Croatian people always lived in states that were more or less imposed on it; the Austro-Hungarian monarchy, both the first and the second Yugoslavia. But throughout there always existed an aspiration on the part of Croats to have -- to achieve their state. That ambition was never satisfied so that it could be taken for granted like it is the case with many European states in which there was never such insistence for independence. But Croatia was in a different position. On one hand, we had Milosevic's pressure, and on the other hand the aspiration to have a state. Would a confederation be an objective? That is a big question. That would probably be a -- not an objective but a means to reach a goal, and the goal was independence."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he says here that the confederation was the means to reach an end and the end was independence.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that this proposal for confederation was a serious one?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not regard it as such, and that's why we refused to accept it as a solution at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What can you say about the mobilisation of reservists, the reasons for the mobilisation in the time and in the conditions in which it was announced?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier in my testimony, I have said several times that the Yugoslav People's Army, despite all the crises and the war in Yugoslavia, especially in Croatia, was decimated. First because Slovenes stopped sending their recruits to the JNA, and they were followed by Croats, then Kosovo Albanians stopped sending their soldiers to the JNA. So the army remained decimated. And this additional mobilisation that was undertaken was a measure to reinforce the army and enable it, but not enable it for offensive action, because I've already said we had never taken such decisions nor did we accept such proposals from the general command staff. This additional mobilisation was only supposed to fulfil the gap that appeared due to the absence of recruits from Slovenia, Croatia, and Kosovo. We also had a special reason to do it, because practically on the 4th of October, Tudjman proclaimed general mobilisation in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the content of the order issued by the Presidency on the 18th of October? Is that the session of the Presidency chaired by Stjepan Mesic held in its full composition in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was that session. We held it before the session of The Hague Conference. I've already said that all eight members of the Presidency were there, as were President Tudjman and you, Mr. Milosevic. The leadership of the international community was there also.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this found in tab 37? It's an order issued by the Presidency of the SFRY held in The Hague, urgent and unconditional cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's very brief. It's in tab 37. It says: "The SFRY Presidency at its session held in The Hague issued an order for an urgent and unconditional cease-fire, said a statement by the chairman of the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs. "The SFRY Presidency issued this order at the beginning of the latest round of the International Conference on Yugoslavia, which is being held at the highest level in the Dutch capital today. "The cease-fire will come into force at 1300 hours Yugoslav time, 1200 hours Central European Time, concludes the statement."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, this is an example. Is there an order somewhere behind this statement, or was the order simply given orally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, Mr. Bonomy, we were all in The Hague when this session was held. I really do not know whether there is a written order. All I know is that as the date was practically the same day, 1300 hours, and the order was issued by telephone to the General Staff to cease urgently and unconditionally all armed activity. And Mr. Tudjman was supposed to issue the same order to his paramilitary formations, but in view of what happened later, I'm not sure that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is a statement by the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs, because they also attended the session. You yourself said van den Broek was there. Was this implemented?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of it was implemented. The first two points of that order which was issued orally were adopted unconditionally. At The Hague Conference, Mr. Tudjman even attempted to impose conditions on point 2 pertaining to lifting the blockade on the barracks. And he was interrupted by Lord Carrington. The conditions he wanted to impose they later did impose, and they did not lift the blockade on the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the statement issued by the SFRY Presidency to the public on the 19th of October, 1991, which is found in tab 38, what is it about? Let's take a look at the first sentence. "The SFRY Presidency, President Tudjman and in the presence of President Milosevic, agreed to issue the following orders to their forces: "Immediate and unconditional cease-fire. "Immediate unblocking of all JNA barracks and JNA facilities in Croatia. "Evacuate all blocked barracks and JNA facilities as soon as possible; evacuate in the direction leading out of Croatia at a pace which is to be agreed upon at the meeting of the tri-party working group in Zagreb," and so on. Please be kind enough to explain this a little bit. The SFRY Presidency and President Tudjman agreed. Is this the essence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I was present there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you were present. I have to point out that throughout this period you played a very prominent role as a strong political authority whenever agreements were made. After the 1st of October, many protagonists of the international community bypassed the SFRY Presidency except when it was not possible to do so. For example, when dealing with the General Staff and the role of the JNA in all this, concluding cease-fires and so on. However, the immediate commander of the armed paramilitary forces in Croatia was President Tudjman, and the Presidency was the other side, the commander of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what was the nature of my presence at these agreements?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, as in some other cases, your presence was your political support as someone with authority to assist the resolution of the crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it aimed at finding a peaceful solution or at raising tensions and conflicts?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that all your efforts, as was also seen after my withdrawal from public and political life, all your efforts were aimed at searching for a peaceful solution, at reaching agreements. And you confirmed this somewhat later in the case of the Vance Plan, because you and Mr. Cyrus Vance advocated the adoption of the peace plan for Croatia and the Krajina, not to mention your later advocation of the Cutileiro plan in Bosnia and other peace proposals that were put forward after I was no longer a member of the Presidency, not to mention Dayton, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was concluded at the session of the 21st of October? It's in tab 39A. The date is the 21st of October, 1991, and it refers to a session of the SFRY Presidency.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At every session, we had occasion to evaluate and to inform the public about every cease-fire that was concluded. As you see, not a single barracks had had the siege lifted. What's more, some of these blockades were even strengthened, and an unusual gesture in diplomatic practice occurred which brings into question the impartiality of the international community. The four principles that Mr. Mesic had put forward at the inaugural session of The Hague Conference on the 7th of September had all been trampled on, especially the third one, which says that every option was to be treated equally and that nothing could be imposed on anyone by force. What is special about this statement is that none of the obligations undertaken by Tudjman at The Hague Conference in relation to the cease-fire had been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the fourth paragraph of this document, you mention a letter that you sent. It says: "It was emphasised at the session that the stipulations of Dr. Franjo Tudjman, president of the Republic of Croatia in commanding the Croatian Armed Forces were unacceptable and contravened the positions and the decision adopted on 18 October 1991 in The Hague. Thus prompted, the SFRY Presidency addressed a letter to Lord Carrington and to the chairman of the EC Council of Ministers van den Broek, pointing out that establishing peace, unfortunately, depends exclusively on the Republic of Croatia implementing agreements, and the behaviour of the Armed Forces. It was also pointed out ..." and so on. And then: "Concern was expressed by the SFRY Presidency because of the situation in which JNA members found themselves in the barracks that were under siege, as well as several members of their families in the Republic of Croatia." What were the responses to this letter that you sent, and were there any positive developments after this or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no positive responses. We really expected that the European Community, as it had promised at the very outset, would use its influence and authority to get the Croatian and Slovenian leaderships to search for political solutions peacefully. None of this was achieved, and I believe that on the 5th of November, at the next session of The Hague Conference, Lord Carrington expressed this very well. He opened the session by stating that the conclusions of the Presidency of the 18th had not been carried out and that Croatia had not lifted the blockade of the military barracks of the JNA on the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what is there in tab 40? What is the content of the Presidency decision on mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a detailed answer to one of the questions put by Judge Bonomy as to who violated the cease-fires. First it speaks of the blockade of the work of the tripartite working group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was that group?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At The Hague Conference of the 18th of October -- or, rather, the Presidency meeting, with all the members present, it was agreed that there should be an unconditional cease-fire and an unconditional lifting of the blockade of the barracks. The modalities and manner of the withdrawal of the JNA from the territory of Croatia was to be discussed at the tripartite working group and agreed in that group. However, the Croatian leadership procrastinated and started imposing conditions on the lifting of the blockade, at the same time failing to respect the cease-fire. And at the beginning of the next page, at the top of the next page, that is at the bottom of page 495 and the beginning of the next page, it says that: "On the -- between the 20th and 21st of October, 1991, members of the armed formations of the Republic of Croatia carried out 34 attacks on JNA units and facilities. In these attacks, 12 JNA members were killed and 37 were wounded, of whom 11 seriously and 26 slightly." There were 24 attacks, that is. Although, according to the decisions from The Hague, Croatia had been required to lift the blockade, it had not done so. Moreover, some garrisons, Zagreb, Karlovac and Sibenik, the blockades have been intensified." "The regular supply of food, electricity and water is still blocked and hindered in the barracks and military facilities of the Republic of Croatia. At a meeting of the tripartite working group in Zagreb, the representative of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia refused to allow the lifting of the blockade of barracks to be placed on the agenda and said that this issue could only be discussed on condition that the evacuation of JNA units from Croatia be discussed first. It is a known fact that under the decision adopted in the Hague, the blockade of the barracks was to be lifted immediately and the blocked barracks and facilities were to be evacuated as soon as possible following a schedule that was to be agreed at a meeting of the tripartite group in Zagreb."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
