utterances.text: In the fourth paragraph, under the title "Obstruction of the work of the tripartite working group," it says: "Members of the armed forces of the SFRY have completely observed the cease-fire order of the 19th of October, 1991. They were never the first to open fire, and they only fired back when they were forced to defend themselves." Is this the situation obtaining at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that throughout this time, throughout the time of the crisis on the territory of the former SFRY, the JNA acted with extreme restraint. Hardly any army anywhere in the world could have shown so much patience and restraint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And towards the end, you say: "The armed forces will comply with the Presidency decision of the 18th of October."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They always found ways to not comply with anything we had agreed on. You can see that here. It says clearly: "The decision adopted in The Hague specified that only the blocked garrisons would be evacuated. The Republic of Croatia, however, still requests that JNA units withdraw from all the garrisons and facilities in the territory of that republic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's dwell briefly on the issue of mobilisation. In paragraph 65, it says: "The Presidency called for the mobilisation of reservists in Serbia and other regions that want to stay in Yugoslavia." That's in this quoted paragraph. Was this full or partial mobilisation? What did it imply? On whose initiative was this decision made? Does what it says in paragraph 65 of the indictment hold water?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is completely incorrect. The Presidency could never have made such a decision, the calling for mobilisation in Serbia. At the request of the staff of the Supreme Command, the Presidency called for raising the manpower levels, because the generation of September and October of 1990 who were completing their training, which lasted for a year, were being sent home. Had we wanted to wage war and engage in offensive action, we would not have let two generations of already trained soldiers go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in this Presidency decision is there any mention made of Serbia? Because in paragraph 65 of the indictment, it said that reservists -- "called for the mobilisation of reservists in Serbia."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There's no formulation like that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Robinson; I omitted to ask that these documents that we've already been through and quoted from be tendered into evidence as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, they may be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Otherwise, on page 68, line 20 of the transcript, it says: "Can a unitary state in Yugoslavia be the same thing?" And I said "Was a unitary state of Serbia and Yugoslavia one and the same thing or can they be one and the same thing?" So I should like to ask that that be put right in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At whose decision was this decision on mobilisation made?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the proposal of the federal secretary for national defence, that is to say general or, rather, the commander of the supreme -- supreme General Staff, Veljko Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 77, now, we have General Kadijevic's statement of the 22nd of October in the Presidency session. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, these proposals by General Kadijevic were adopted by the Presidency, were they? Which were they? Were they the three adopted decisions that were incorporated into the decision we quoted earlier on?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, the decisions made by the Presidency of the 22nd, were they offensive in nature, of an offensive nature or defensive in nature?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please repeat your answer. The interpreter did not hear it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that it is quite clear from the formulation and the contents of these proposals for measures to be taken that they were of a defensive nature, not offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, did you take part at The Hague Conference on Yugoslavia in the autumn of 1991?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was -- there were a number of Hague conferences. I took part in three of them. The first inaugural meeting of The Hague Conference, on the 7th of September, I attended that one, and the 18th of October meeting as well, and the 5th of November meeting, 1991. I attended those three.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was your attitude towards the proposals presented by Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I, for example, stemming from my own personal views and positions and my desire to settle the conflict peacefully, to settle our political crisis peacefully, but also stemming from our right that if certain republics wish to secede, then those who wish to remain living in a common state, joint state, should be given equal treatment, at least equal treatment as those who wish to secede and are seceding in a forcible manner. So it was along these lines and in that sense that I was rather reserved vis-a-vis the first chapter of The Hague document. And let me also say that Lord Carrington at the very outset did not attend -- invite the Presidency of the SFRY to attend the conference at all, and then we sent September a sharp-worded letter of caution in which we stated that even if the presidents of the republics did agree, that the decision -- that the decisions would not be fully valid because it is not up to the presidents of the republics to decide such matters but it was up to the Presidency as the head of state to decide such matters. Now, the first chapter of The Hague document left open the possibility in practical terms that of the six republics of the former SFRY six independent and sovereign states be automatically constituted. Yugoslavia would be wiped off the political map at The Hague Conference. Serbia and Montenegro already at that time expressed their desire to continue living together in a joint state, and at The Hague Conference, similarly, that right of theirs was challenged precisely by the leaders of the secessionist republics, and thereby the third principle was trampled upon, the third principle from the joint appearance that Mr. Mesic publicised at the inaugural conference of the 7th of September in The Hague, and that was that all options should be taken on an equal footing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the amendments tendered by the then president of the Presidency of Montenegro, Momir Bulatovic and I myself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that amendment followed on the steps of the 18th Presidency session held on the 18th. Mr. Carrington didn't -- Lord Carrington did not give me the floor, did not allow me to speak at The Hague Conference, and after that meeting there was an amendment that followed. In fact, there were two amendments. One was sent by you and Mr. Bulatovic, and the second amendment was sent in by the Montenegrin Presidency, but the substance of those two amendments was almost identical. It said that, along with acceptance of everything stated in the first chapter of The Hague document, you went on to propose that there should be another point included which would read roughly as follows -- I have it somewhere but to paraphrase it, there was just one sentence, and it was this: To recognise the rights of those who wish to continue living in a joint state to do so, just as the right of those secede was recognised; that they be treated equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So to be treated equally, those who wished to step down from Yugoslavia and those who wished to remain in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was that something that was not principled, to ask for the same treatment, those wishing to leave and those wishing to stay? Was there anything wrong with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a very principled stand and position. And let me say again, the position adopted unilaterally -- or, rather, unitedly in the -- that was a stand that was fully endorsed by the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you mean the Presidency of this SFRY, including Mesic as a member and all the rest, accepted that position whereas later on this was not incorporated into the Hague document, and we asked for the equal treatment of those who wished to remain as well as those who wished to leave. That was rejected.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They rejected it and I had the impression that Lord Carrington was willing to adopt that amendment which would provide for equal treatment for those wishing to secede and those wishing to stay in the same state, however it was rejected -- I don't know who, but it was rejected by the republics and leaderships of the republics which had opted for secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 85 of this alleged Croatian indictment, it says the following: "As of the 1 August 1991 until at least June 1992 --" that is to say it was the period where you were -- you led the Presidency; is that right? It says in Croatia there was a situation of armed conflict, and there's a full stop there. "Up to the 7th of October, 1991, that conflict was an internal one. From the 8th of October, 1991, an international armed conflict and partial occupation existed in the Republic of Croatia." Now what is it that happened on the 7th or 8th of October, 1991, that the situation in Croatia which you've just described to us in all the events suddenly turned into an international armed conflict and partial occupation, as it says here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the 8th of October, the Croatian leadership proclaimed that the deadline had expired, the three-month deadline that had been granted, it had been an erroneous interpretation of the Brioni Declaration, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When we looked into the Brioni Declaration, it had nothing to do with Croatia, those three months.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but at the time they proclaimed their independence -- they had proclaimed their independence, and this formulation given in the indictment read out by you a moment ago is highly incorrect and actually nonsensical, all the more so since in the indictment itself there is a separate count or paragraph - unless I'm much mistaken, I think it's 110 or 109 - in which it is claimed that Yugoslavia had existed up until the 27th of April, 1992, when the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was replaced by the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. So in the indictment, to claim that up until the 8th of October, 1991, that conflict had an internal -- was of an internal nature and after the 8th of October international nature, although I'm not a legal man myself or an expert in international law, as far as I'm concerned that is quite nonsensical.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know in what manner the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia reacted to the decision taken by the Sabor of the Republic of Croatia, or its Assembly, the decision on the dissolution of the state ties between the SFRY adopted on the 8th of October, 1991, the unilateral act of the 8th of October? How did the Constitutional Court react to that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Constitutional Court of Yugoslavia, unless I'm much mistaken, on the 12th of November, or around that date, or the 20th of November perhaps, discussed the issue and decided and ruled that that was unconstitutional and invalid, what the Croatian leadership had adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at tab 86 now, please, and in that tab you will find the decision taken by the Sabor or Croatian Assembly, where it says the 8th of October, 1991, where it says Croatia is abolishing all state relationships which, based with the other republics and provinces made up the SFRY up until that date. So that's the decision. I don't want to quote it in full, but you have the document of it there and it is tab 86. And in that same tab you have the decision on the constitutionality -- on assessing the constitutionality of Croatia's decision to sever ties.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to tab 86, I must say I don't have that tab in my binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a technical error then on my part, I assume.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do have it, I do have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Tell us now, please, in view of the text of the decision by the Constitutional Court, who moved proceedings before the Constitutional Court against the Republic of Croatia and its severance of any ties with the SFRY and the decision adopted on the 8th of October?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Federal Executive Council that took those steps and initiated those proceedings, led by the president or, rather, the Prime Minister, Ante Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, please, to the best of your knowledge and your understandings, according to the attitude of the Presidency, did the armed conflict indeed change its nature when Croatia proclaimed its independence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said, although I'm not an expert in legal matters, any form, especially not international law, I would say that that observation seems to me to be slightly ludicrous, although I'm a layman, as I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, the JNA was there. It was in its garrisons. It was stationed throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia. How long did the JNA and prior to that the army of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia spend on that territory, the territory for which it is claimed the international armed conflict broke out there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the army was deployed throughout the territory and therefore also on the territory of Croatia for a full 70 years, when the first Yugoslavia was in existence and when the second Yugoslavia came into being; throughout that time. And on the 8th of October, it was still the sole constitutional armed force of the country, the country that was Yugoslavia still.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the agreement to withdraw the JNA from Croatia and the applications of that agreement, its implementation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't have the intention in Croatia or anywhere else to impose a solution by using the JNA on anyone, but to all intents and purposes in Croatia, for example, and at the beginning in Slovenia and as later happened in Bosnia where we did intend to pull out and withdraw certain units of the Yugoslav People's Army, we were prevented in doing so because those units of the JNA, which in peacetime were to be found on the territory of Croatia, had been blocked for several months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, a moment ago you told us how long the army remained on the territory of Croatia. Tell me now according to the Presidency decision and attitude and your personal attitude, could the JNA, that JNA that had been there for decades, could it, on the basis of the fact that Croatia had proclaimed its decision, which we can see was rejected by the Constitutional Court, but based on Croatia's proclamations, could it automatically become an occupying force?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it could not because, according to the constitution, it was the sole constitutional armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it found itself there, it happened to be there. These people took their decision and suddenly it had the role of an occupier, having been there for 17 years.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only was it not an occupier in those barracks, but it was itself occupied by Croatia's paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But was it able physically to withdraw?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's why I'm saying it could not have physically withdrawn, because it was under a blockade. It was under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 108 of the Croatian indictment, we have mention of the fact that Tudjman, Kadijevic, and Milosevic were in Geneva with Vance. The agreement called for the lifting of blockades of the barracks and the withdrawal of the JNA forces from Croatia, and something is quoted there. It says: "units under their command, control, or political influence." That is the quotation. Can you explain that to us, please?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's the same explanation that I gave a moment ago when we were discussing the Presidency meeting prior to The Hague Conference on the 18th of October, when they were in full composition. In those agreements at the time, we had the participation on behalf of the SFRY, Mr. Kadijevic; and on behalf of the Croatian military forces, you had Mr. Tudjman attending. And similarly, as insistence was made then on this occasion too, and many times later, insistence was made on your participation regardless of the fact that in the formal sense, in the formal legal sense, you did not have the competence and authority to do so. However, all the actors in the international community that were included in trying to solve the Yugoslav crisis and trying to assist in it, their attitude towards you was towards a man who enjoyed high political authority and influence. So I think that this formulation reflects that, because the political influence is stressed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we'll take the break now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what is the purpose, the meaning of this agreement, especially in the part that relates to the lifting of the blockade of the barracks and the withdrawal of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic purpose of that agreement is to finally start doing what was envisaged by the previous 14 agreements. Every one of those agreements began with that demand, and it was a requirement for bringing UN peacekeepers. If you mean the Cyrus Vance agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And speaking of an army that's been in a territory for 70 years and that is currently under blockade in its barracks and is unable to move, can it be considered an occupier?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a bit ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And can Krajina Serbs be considered occupiers in the area of Krajina? Let's say a Krajina Serb who leaves his house in which his family had been living for hundreds of years. If he leaves his house to protect his family from attackers coming from hundreds kilometres away, can he be considered an occupier as opposed to the person who is attacking him who is treated as a fighter against occupation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a well known fact that Krajina Serbs had lived there for hundreds of years. So that's a ridiculous proposition, like many others that can be found in the indictment. I had the impression, reading the indictment, that this -- if a tsunami had happened before the indictment was written, it would have been one of the charges against you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was the last time Mesic chaired a Presidency session in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time that Mr. Mesic chaired a full Presidency session was on the 18th of October in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us play just another brief clip from that television programme that was shown on Montenegro television.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you play the clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] You say that Croatia had ambitions to create its own independent state. Do you think that the fear of Serbs from that independent Croatia was justified in view of the history, the Jasenovac camp, the Independent State of Croatia, the iconography, and the rhetorics of the Croatian Democratic Union, especially if we bear in mind Tudjman's statement?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The sound is gone. "[Voiceover] Well, that statement of his will continue to be paid for by our people. A person, especially a president of the state, shouldn't even think that, let alone say it aloud. I have to say, for the sake of truth, on one side there were misgivings among the Serbs, and that fear was of a recreation of that independent state of Croatia that was everything but independent. It was a creature of the Third Reich, the powers of the axis; Germany and Italy."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to hear?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you comment on what he said?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here, answering the question from the anchor whether Serbs in Croatia had reasons to fear, Mr. Mesic confirmed that they did indeed have reason to be afraid because there were many things that reminded them of what had happened in the Independent State of Croatia, when Croatia was not actually a state but a creature of the Third Reich, as he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that he chaired a session on the 18th of October.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And we saw in the paragraph that was quoted that on the 7th of October some international armed conflict happened. Explain to me, therefore, how is it possible for a president of an occupied state to chair a session of the Presidency of the -- which is a Supreme Commander of the occupying force?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then please read the second half of the penultimate paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... occupying force, because an occupying army is a particular concept in the law of armed conflict. But as used in the indictment, does it mean anything other than that the Serb forces were there? It's not clear to me, because you have used the term several times, so you attach importance to it, and I'm not sure whether that significance is to be gathered from the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Robinson, paragraph 85 says: "From 8 October 1991, there was international armed conflict and partial occupation in the Republic of Croatia." I don't attach importance to it because it's correct but because it's absurd, because it begs the question of whether an army that has been legally on the territory of its own state for 70 years can become an occupier overnight and whether the local people can become occupiers on their own doorstep. How can it be used in a serious text -- at least, Mr. Nice pretends its serious. How can that term be used if it's pure absurd?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. It just wasn't clear to me the sense in which you were using it. For example, in paragraph 109, there's a reference to "the areas occupied by Serb forces." And further on, there is a reference to "the Serb-occupied areas," and "the territory of the RSK remained under Serb occupation." It's not clear to me whether all of that translates into an occupying army, but we need not debate that now. Please proceed with the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We can also ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it under some sort of Serb occupation; and if so, in what way?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say what I have already repeated several times here. In the area of Serbian Krajina in Croatia, where the majority population was Serb, the Serbs had lived several hundred years. I don't know how it is even possible to talk about those Serbs there who had their property, houses, as somebody who occupied the territory. That's one. And second, in those places where there was JNA presence, we cannot talk about the JNA as an occupying force unless we accept the language of Mr. Mesic and others from the secessionist republics who called the Yugoslav People's Army an occupying army. But in practical terms, until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in paragraph 109, the line I just read: "The territory of the RSK remained under Serb occupation." I think "occupation" there, it seems to me, means habitation. Well, on the face of it, but it's a matter to be determined.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that there was Serb habitation there for centuries is not in dispute. But in my terminology and my language, "occupation" means something quite different. If that is considered occupation when I occupy my house, then your interpretation would be correct. Then it is not something that could be a charge against someone. How can somebody be charged with occupying their own home? Why did it find its place here at all then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please proceed. Proceed with the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, please read the second half of the penultimate paragraph and the last paragraph on page 294 of Mesic's book. That's tab 73. What does Mesic say, how he participated in the convoy of ships to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the page number again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Page 294 of his book. Read the second half of the penultimate paragraph, beginning with the words: "As a result of the commitment of the most prominent intellectuals ..." and the last paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "As a result of the commitment of the most prominent intellectuals of Croatia that was unequivocally supported by the humane world but also due to the chauvinism of the unpoisoned personality of Belgrade, a humanitarian convoy of ships and vessels was organised to set out on the 28th of October from Rijeka, make a stopover in Zadar, Split, and Korcula and set in, if everything goes according to plan, at Dubrovnik on the morning of the 30th of October. I decided to join the convoy to give my support to general solidarity, but also because somehow I was number one in the Supreme Command."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about this. He says he was man number one in the Supreme Command, that he was indeed president of the Presidency, so it's not in dispute. How is it possible then for the president of an occupied state, as he put it, to be at the same time number one of the Supreme Command of the occupying force and to set in to places held by that occupying army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is pure nonsense. And although you are telling me I'm going into too much detail in my testimony, but I have to say that while Mr. Mesic was president of the Presidency, he was president of the Presidency as long as it suited him. Whenever it didn't suit him, he appeared paralysed and disabled from performing that function. In all this time as a president of the Presidency, did not have any powers circumventing the authorities of the full Presidency to go and make any international visits. But he did go to Vienna, Berlin, Brussels, Washington, London, The Hague, and he appeared everywhere as president of the Presidency of the SFRY, although both under the constitution and under the rules of procedure of the Presidency, he did not have such powers. So now when he was supposed to join the convoy to Dubrovnik, and he says himself he was bringing volunteers, he presents himself as number one of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how is it possible for this number one man in the Supreme Command to go there, and he is at the same time president of an occupied state? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you read the heading and the first few lines on page 305. It says: "Dismantled Yugoslavia disappears even formally."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 305?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 305. What does he say? Read the title and the first and penultimate points of the sub-heading.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said: "Dismantled Yugoslavia disappears even formally. The 4th of November until 5th December 1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Mesic claims that Yugoslavia disappeared by 5th December 1991. This indictment claims that as of 8th October there existed armed conflict and occupation. What is true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither is true. What is true is paragraph 110 or 109. That's where I agree with the Prosecution. "Yugoslavia existed as an internationally recognised state until 27th April 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what does Mesic say? You told us in what capacity he travelled to various places; Luxembourg, Belgium, France, his last travels as president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he allegedly travelled as president of the Presidency of the SFRY, but from everything he said and from his book, the purpose of his travels was to advance the interests of the Croatian leadership, to secede from Yugoslavia as soon as possible, and to achieve Croatian independence. So he was actually engaging in anti-constitutional activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did the Croatian Assembly withdraw Stjepan Mesic from his post as president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it happened on the 5th of December, 1991, in the Croatian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the 5th of December. In what way did Stjepan Mesic make his last report to the Croatian Assembly about the Presidency session? That's the 5th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] ... became a self-reliant and independent Croatian state. I have performed my task. Yugoslavia is no more. Thank you very much."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did he say here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I have performed my task. Yugoslavia is no more. Thank you very much."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he has performed his task and Yugoslavia is no more. The other day you said here that the title of his first book was "How I Toppled Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he himself said, and then Genscher told him it would not be received well. That's why he changed the title to "How We Toppled Yugoslavia," and then in the final version it was, "How Yugoslavia Was Toppled."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this title has its evolution, but now we've seen the original footage, where he says, "I have performed my task. Yugoslavia is no more." Let us now look at a clip where he speaks in the Sabor, the Croatian parliament, and it's here on page 296, where I say: "[Previous translation continues] ... [In English] confidence, and you made a notorious statement to the effect that you -- that you -- I have performed my task. Yugoslavia is no more. "Is it so, Mr. Mesic?" [Interpretation] I'll jump over what I asked because we have seen this on the footage. His reply: "[In English] Excellent question. I will explain what this was about. The Croatian parliament elected me to be Croatian member of the Presidency of Yugoslavia." [Interpretation] Then he goes on to explain how he was elected. We've been through all that. And he says: "[In English] ... decision of its independence, Croatia, in agreement with the international community, postponed its secession from Yugoslavia by three months. This time period had elapsed. Yugoslavia no longer existed. The federal institutions were no longer functioning. I returned to Zagreb, and that's precisely what I said, because I did not go to Belgrade to open up a house painting business. I went there as a member of Presidency of Yugoslavia. Since Yugoslavia no longer exists and Presidency no longer exists, I perform the task entrusted to me by Croatian parliament and was reporting back, ready to take up a different office." "Very well, Mr. Mesic. This is truly worth your admiration, your explanation of what you said, but you haven't told me whether you actually said, 'I have performed my task. Yugoslavia is no more.' "The accused is a lawyer, he understands very well what I'm talking about. My task was to represent Croatia in Federal Presidency." [Interpretation] And then I say there's no need for him to mention that. Well, you have now seen the footage. Is what he says in his testimony correct or is what is correct what we see in the footage?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's no doubt that what we have seen in the footage is true. On that same occasion, Mr. Domljan, who was the speaker of parliament, the Croatian parliament at the time, literally said, I quote -- it's on page 320 of Mesic's book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Chamber will make up its mind as to what is true, what is credible, so move on to another matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Professor Kostic, how is it possible for a representative of an occupied state for a full two months after the so-called occupation remains the head of state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's not a permissible question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We will then move on. Of what Yugoslav republic was General Kadijevic a representative when he was elected as secretary of defence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And until what time did he hold that post?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until -- well, just before the end of 1992, he announced that, for reasons of health, he had to resign. Officially, it was the 8th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So how is it possible for a minister from an occupied state to be at the head of an army that is actually occupying that state?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no question [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was he?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a minister. He was a member of the Federal Executive Council, which is practically the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who was at its head at the time mentioned in the indictment, the 8th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Ante Markovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be a pause between question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic and the witness, the interpreter is asking you to pause between the question and the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Also from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Until when was Markovic the Prime Minister of the federal government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I think it was around the 20th or the 22nd of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember why Ante Markovic resigned on the 20th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Markovic resigned because he did not agree with the other members of the government about the federal budget for 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted that on the record. How was it possible for the representative of an occupied state to be the Prime Minister of the government of an occupying state?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have no answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer that. Don't answer that question. Next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 110 of the Croatia indictment, it says: "The SFRY existed as a sovereign state until the 27th of April, 1992, when the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was adopted, replacing the constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia of 1974." Is this correct, or what it says in paragraph 85, or can both statements be correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not a question for the witness to answer. This is all about the statehood of Croatia, the legal consequences of certain moves that were made. That's not for the witness. We are actually wasting a lot of time now, for almost an hour on this, and I think it should really be stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That issue is not, as the Prosecutor said, for this witness. Move on, Mr. Milosevic, and we really need to make some progress. How much longer will you be with this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think at least a whole day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You will bear in mind what I said to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am bearing it in mind, but I think that this a witness is very important. He was at the head of the Presidency practically throughout this whole relevant time period. That's why I feel his testimony is relevant on all points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Professor Kostic, what did the SFRY Presidency put forward in the information of the 15th of November, 1991, presented to the Assembly of Yugoslavia regarding the resolution of the Yugoslav crisis?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I submitted an expose to the Yugoslav parliament. Not my personal view but the assessment of all of us in the Presidency, and we communicated to them our assessment of this situation which was causing us extreme concern. All the efforts towards peace that we had invested and everything we had done through General Kadijevic, who acted pursuant to our orders, was yielding no results. At the same time, we stated that at the Presidency level and at the level of the federal government work was being carried out on parallel tracks. Mr. Ante Markovic as the Prime Minister, and Mr. Budimir Loncar as the foreign minister were failing to carry out their constitutional obligations referring to the preservation of Yugoslavia, as opposed to Mr. Gracanin and Mr. Kadijevic who were the minister of the interior and the minister of defence respectively and who were acting in accordance with their constitutional duties. We expressed our view that this was a very grave situation and that a way out had to be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the main point of the letter sent to Lord Carrington on the 19th of December regarding the Arbitration Commission by the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency expressed its disagreement with its -- with the assessment made by the Arbitration Commission simply because the commission failed to take into account the basic provisions of the Yugoslav constitution which were then valid and in force, one of which was the right of each nation to self-determination, including the right to secession. The Arbitration Commission in this particular case did not recognise the right of the Serbian people in the Republic of Croatia, although even according to the constitution of Croatia, this nation was a constituent nation of the Croatian state until Tudjman's government and the HDZ removed it from the Croatian constitution and gave it the status of an ethnic minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did the SFRY Presidency express itself on the 15th of December, 1991, regarding the recognition of Croatia and Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency evaluated this as a conscious attack on Yugoslavia, as a move leading to further escalation of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How did the Presidency of the SFRY express itself on the 17th of December, 1991, regarding the criteria of the European Community on the recognition of new states?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the same way the Presidency expressed its dissatisfaction, because throughout this time, the time of the Yugoslav crisis, practically until November the European Community had publicly supported the preservation of the territorial integrity of Yugoslavia and the comprehensive solution of the Yugoslav crisis, but evidently when Germany finally managed to impose its own standpoint on the other members of the European Community, a turnaround came about and the European Community completely changed its standpoint. On the 17th of December, it publicly announced and communicated the criteria to the Yugoslav republics, encouraging them to queue up and apply for independence with the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you explained this at length yesterday, so we will not dwell upon it any longer. What was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Professor, if you could explain to me in brief terms the difference of being a constituent people on the one hand and being an ethnic minority on the other hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the Yugoslav constitution and according to the constitutions of each individual republic, it was defined. There were two kinds of status, that of a constituent nation and that of an ethnic minority. In Croatia, the two constituent nations of the Croatian Republic were the Croats and the Serbs. All the others were designated as ethnic minorities. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was expressly stated that Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a socialist republic within SFRY, was constituted by three constituent nations; the Muslims, the Serbs, and the Croats. And this was in order of their numbers. The difference between the way constituent nations were treated as opposed to ethnic minorities - and I'm referring to Yugoslavia - and this may not be a legal explanation, but the difference was that members of nations that already had a nation state somewhere could not become constituent nations in a Yugoslav republic. For example, the numerous Albanian population living in Kosovo, although they were more numerous than the Serbs were in Croatia, had the status of an ethnic minority on the territory of Serbia, because there was a nation state for Albanians in Albania. Serbs lived in Croatia and they had the status of a constituent nation. The provisions in the constitution of the SFRY and also in the constitutions of the various republics clearly prescribed that the interests of each constituent nation had to be taken into account. One constituent nation, or two constituent nations in the case of Bosnia, could not make any decisions without the approval of the remaining constituent people. There could be no out-voting. I don't know if this answer is clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As long as the rights of the minority people are respected, or to put it differently, unless they are discriminated, I don't see much difference between constituent people and minority.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your permission, Mr. Kwon, had you perhaps lived in the territory of the Balkans at any time, and had you by chance lived in that area where the Serb people lived in Croatia, for example, and if you had experienced everything that that peoples had experienced in World War II, then you would understand that difference far better. It is precisely because of that unfortunate destiny and fate that the Serb people suffered during World War II that most -- this most probably had an effect and the Serb people in the constitution were a constituent nation together with the Croatian people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understand that. My question was rather a practical one. What is the difference in terms of the rights they have in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think I've already told you: All matters of fate and destiny that are decided must be decided with the acquiescence of both or all three constituent peoples. And in cases of national minorities, that is not required, not called for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that is -- is that provided by the provision of constitutional law -- constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It must be defined -- defined in the constitution. I can look for it. The Croatian constitution and the Bosnia-Herzegovina constitution, where that is stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One -- one of the attributes you ascribe to a constituent people is the right to self-determination and secession. Now, does that apply to a constituent people as a constituent people of a republic separately from its application to that constituent nation or people as part of the federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I'm afraid that is too complex a question for me to answer, but I'll do my best to answer on the basis of practice, because I'm not a lawyer myself. On the basis of practice and the experience we gained according to the Yugoslav constitution and respect for the Yugoslav constitution and the republican constitutions by the same token, both in the Yugoslav constitution and in the republican constitutions, where there are a number of constituent peoples making up a territorial whole, the basic principle was that one nation, regardless of its number and size, can do anything to the detriment of another people, make any fateful decisions. In the case of Croatia, what happened was this: The Croatian people to all intents and purposes by adopting the new constitution threw out the Serbs, left out the Serbs. They were no longer this constituent people. The same thing happened in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask then, to just clear one thing to which I think the answer is obvious but it would be helpful to have it on the record: How many constituent peoples made up the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Republic of Serbia was made up just by one constituent peoples, and that was the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But since there were no other constituent peoples in the Republic of Serbia, what was decided was that within the composition of Serbia you had two autonomous provinces; the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija and the autonomous province of Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask us to hear a brief statement made by Lord Carrington which I think would fit in very well here within the context of our discussions and deliberations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm advised that the booth is looking for the tape. So move on, and we can come back to it. Oh, it's there now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "This was a war that European leaders believed could have been avoided. "The Bosnian Serbs, until comparatively recently, have been in the majority in Bosnia, and then the Muslims, who had a very much higher birth rate, became predominant, the majority population, and this of course was something very hard for the Serbs to swallow, and they made it abundantly plain very early on that they were not prepared to accept the situation in which there was an independent Bosnia under the constitution which then prevailed. And indeed under the constitution which then prevailed, it was not -- it was illegal for Izetbegovic to declare independence because any constitutional change of that magnitude had to be agreed by all three parties."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't hear the soundtrack. I was just listening to the interpretation into Serbian. I don't know whether you were able to hear what he said in English. So what is it that Lord Carrington says; that the proclamation of independence was illegal because something like that had to be agreed upon between the three constituent peoples. So when we're talking about the rights of constituent peoples or a constituent people, the right to self-determination, was it possible or was it legal to change the constitution or legal status of a republic without the acquiescence and agreement of the constituent peoples?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. And I think that Lord Carrington put this very properly: It was illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I hope that this explanation given by Lord Carrington has served to clarify your dilemmas.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With your indulgence, Mr. Milosevic, may I be allowed to say something further? Bosnia-Herzegovina also had a collective Presidency, a collective head of state for the republic, and that Presidency was left. They left because by the representative members of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina who were the Serb representatives. But then a double yardstick was applied. Alija Izetbegovic was treated throughout by the international community as president of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it never entered into anybody's head in the international community that that -- to refer to that Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a Rump Presidency because it didn't have any Serb representatives in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Although Lord Carrington also says that the decision was illegal.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And he was the chairman of the Conference on Yugoslavia, the presiding officer. But let's move on to the next topic. What is the meaning and substance of the SFRY Presidency to the Security Council in December 1991, 21st of December?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we finally came to realise that all our efforts were not bearing fruit and that the European Community was not giving us the support and assistance the European Community had -- as a mediator, good services had offered us at the very beginning and we received evermore open criticism to the effect that the Yugoslav People's Army and the use of the Yugoslav People's Army was aimed at taking over territory, we in the Presidency arrived at the conclusion that the best solution would be that we as a Presidency, as the Yugoslav state Presidency and the Supreme Command, we address the UN Secretary-General and the Security Council and to have them send the UN peace forces, which would be deployed in the crisis spots in Croatia with the basic task of physically protecting the Serb population living in those areas. And in that case, the Yugoslav People's Army could withdraw from those areas, because it was accused of being an occupying force. So what we wanted was that the UN peacekeepers should take over the role of physical protection for the population, because we considered that the Croatian paramilitary formations would not attack the UN peace forces as they had been attacking the JNA. So that a truce could be established, a cease-fire, and then given those peaceful conditions without mutual conflicts, a political settlement could be sought.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On that same day, the 20th of December, you sent an opinion by the Presidency to the Arbitration Commission having to do with the right to self-determination. That was the subject; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the reason for that? You wrote to the Security Council to send in UN forces, and what did you write to the Arbitration Commission?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we said that we disagreed, and we said that the Arbitration Commission failed to take into account the constitutional solutions that we had adopted linked to the rights of each constituent people to self-determination to the right to secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did it say in all the constitutions of Yugoslavia? Did it say the people's of Yugoslavia, the nations of Yugoslavia, is that what it said?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the peoples of Yugoslavia, that's what it said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who were the peoples of Yugoslavia or the nations of Yugoslavia that were enumerated in all the country's constitutions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people of Yugoslavia that were listed in all the constitutions were as follows: The Slovenes, the Croats, the Serbs, the Montenegrins, and the Macedonians. And from 1962 onwards, I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was a little later. It was a little later.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyway, the Yugoslav coat of arms had five torches, symbolising the five constituent peoples. Somewhat later, I think that was in -- in the mid 1960s, the then party and state leadership of Yugoslavia recognised the right of the Muslims as a national right, as a separate entity. So that the Muslims too in Yugoslavia gained the status of a constituent people. And from that moment on, in future constitutions the Muslims are also listed as a constituent people. Of course, that was on a religious basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was a little later on, but never mind, it's not relevant to what we're discussing here I won't go into that now, but tell us, at whose initiative was the Vance Plan adopted?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Vance Plan was adopted -- or what brought about its adoption was the initiative of the four-member Yugoslav state Presidency, which was in function as of the 3rd of October and continued working faced with the situation of imminent threat of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 72 do we have a letter by the Yugoslav state Presidency that was sent to the president of the Security Council, inviting the Security Council to send peacekeepers to the country? I think you quoted it in your book on page 133 to 135. It's in tab 72, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what was it you asked for at the time? What did you request?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you want to read it -- me to read it all out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. Just the elementary points.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we described the situation, the lack of respect of all the truces agreed upon, and we highlight the blockade, and failure to comply by Croatia and the Croatian paramilitaries and forces, we said the following: With our invitation, or in view of everything that was happening and in our call to have the UN peacekeepers come to the Republic of Croatia in the border belt between the territories that are populated by majority Serb population and territories where there is a majority Croat population, we say in such a way that the UN forces would create a buffer zone and separate the two conflicting sides until a peaceful and just solution and one based on international law is found along with the engagement of the United Nations, until the Yugoslav crisis is solved in that way, thereby creating the necessary prerequisites for the Presidency of the SFRY as the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the SFRY makes a decision to disengage the Yugoslav People's Army in preventing inter-ethnic clashes and conflicts on the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there you call for the UN peacekeepers to be sent in and the disengagement of the army in view of the fact that the UN peacekeepers would take on the role of protecting the population. Now, when was the plan drawn up, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the plan was drawn up, I think, during the month of December that was. And on the 2nd of January, 1992, I think it was, Mr. Cyrus Vance informed the public that the plan had been drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the attitude of the authorities in Serbia? My own attitude towards the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was undivided support for the Vance Plan, without any reservations whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the attitude of the overall -- the entire Presidency towards Vance's plan? This was the initiative. Now, once the plan had been compiled, what did the Presidency think about it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the basic substance of Vance's plan was to establish a truce, to establish the physical protection of population in the area; therefore, the Presidency was in favour. So the sense and substance of Vance Plan coincided with our views as to how conditions could be created for a political settlement to be found in peaceful conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me another thing: This striving to have the UN peacekeepers sent to the country, can that be linked up with any intention or intent to expel the Croats from some territory and then to attach that territory to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's nonsense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't answer that. Those are matters for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any resistance to having the Vance Plan adopted?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that at the very outset there was great resistance to the Vance Plan by most of the leadership in the Serbian Krajinas on the territory of Croatia. However, with patient politicking and numerous efforts at persuading them and explaining to them what it was all about -- we had several meetings, one went on for 40 hours, a Presidency meeting with the most responsible representatives of the Serbs from Krajina -- all of them ended up by accepting the plan with the exception of Mr. Milan Babic. And I have to say that at the time during that -- those many hours of persuasion to have them accept the plan, we were greatly assisted by the gentleman from the leadership of Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina because they took part in the negotiations. And they were Mr. Radovan Karadzic, for instance, Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Krajisnik, and Mrs. Plavsic. Out of all of those, it was only Mrs. Plavsic who expressed her non-agreement with the plan and gave her support to Milan Babic. Of course, there were also the corps commanders such as Ratko Mladic. He was commander of the Drina Corps at the time. He also lent his support to the plan, and as a general and as a military commander, he cautioned what a war conflict would mean and the sufferings that that would bring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And on at that note, we must end the day's proceedings. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, do we know which witness is coming tomorrow? Should we check, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, with your permission, the witness testifying tomorrow will be Ms. Eve-Ann Prentice. Eve-Ann Prentice. I have to apologise to the witness for interposing Ms. Prentice. I have already explained why I asked her to be interposed, so I apologise to the witness for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will she be here all day, all three sessions?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, I assume she'll have to take up the whole day with the cross-examination as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn. And you should be back on Monday, the 6th, not tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If Your Honour thought I was looking a little concerned, I was just wondering whether it would be prudent to ensure that this witness is available. I don't know what the scope of Ms. or Mrs. Prentice's evidence is going to be nor, thus, how long I will wish to spend with her in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in that event, then, you should make yourself available for tomorrow. The Victims and Witnesses Unit will see to that. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 3rd day of February, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
